Ten thousand elements on screen. Drawdy still draws frames a second.

We opened one 10,000-element board in Drawdy, Excalidraw and tldraw, then had a script pan and zoom across it. With the whole board in view, Excalidraw drew frames a second and tldraw .

One second of panning

Each tick is a frame the editor finished during one second of panning with all 10,000 elements in view. The screen refreshes times a second, so ticks is the most any editor can show.

Simulation: each panel moves the same drawing and updates it only as often as that editor did in the test above.

Six measurements

Median of runs per editor. Hover a bar for its frame times.

about capacity

tldraw stops at 4,000 shapes per page by default, so the 10,000-element board does not open in a stock tldraw editor. For this test we raised its maxShapesPerPage option to 10,000. Excalidraw opened all 10,000 without changes. A Drawdy board holds up to 10,000 elements.

What was on screen

Each editor right after opening the board, zoomed to fit. All three drew all 10,000 elements.

How we measured

  • Machine. , with the GPU on, a 1440 × 900 window at 2× (Retina), Hz display.
  • Board. 10,000 elements in a 125 × 80 grid: 30% rectangles, 15% ellipses, 10% diamonds, 15% arrows, 15% text labels and 15% pen strokes, a third of the shapes filled. One fixed seed, so every editor gets the same positions, sizes and colours.
  • Opening. Each editor starts from a JSON string in its own format and its own importer: Excalidraw's restoreElements, Drawdy's Excalidraw paste importer, tldraw's createShapes. Timed from handing over the string until three frames in a row finish under 20 ms.
  • Editors. Drawdy at commit (the engine drawdy.io runs, without the app's toolbar), @excalidraw/excalidraw and tldraw with their default UI. Production builds.
  • Camera. A script moves each editor's camera through its public API on identical paths: circling with the whole board in view; zooming between fit-to-board and 100% in 0.4 s bursts with 0.25 s pauses; and panning at 100% zoom at about 1,700 px/s. 0.5 s warm-up, then 6 s measured. Fresh browser per run, editors in rotating order.
  • Frame rate counts the frames the browser actually produced (requestAnimationFrame callbacks). Longest freeze is the slowest single frame across the three camera tests. Memory is the increase in the tab's renderer and GPU process footprint, the figure Activity Monitor shows, measured after loading and a garbage collection.

Why Drawdy stays fast

Drawdy draws the board into cached 1,024 px tiles at a few zoom levels, and finds elements through a spatial index written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly. Panning places tiles that are already drawn instead of redrawing 10,000 shapes. While you zoom it scales the tiles it has, then redraws them sharp 80 ms after the zoom stops; the burst test includes those redraws.

Bars on this page are drawn to exact length. Only the frames, ticks and notes are hand-drawn.
